newsitem.title: POLAND: OECD sees Poland's GDP up 5 pct in 1997 and 1998.
newsitem.headline: OECD sees Poland's GDP up 5 pct in 1997 and 1998.

text.p: The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) said on Thursday it expected Poland's economy to grow by about five percent in 1997 and 1998 after a six percent rise in 1996, on strong industrial growth.

"In the first quarter of 1997 industrial sales were up almost eight percent over a year earlier, boding well for the achievement of a growth rate in real GDP of around five percent in 1997," the report said.

"The magnitude of the additions to capacity in 1995-1996 suggests this pace could be sustained in 1998, provided that external demand, particularly in the European Union, is sufficiently vigorous," it said.

The OECD report also said Poland's 1997 inflation target of 13 percent in year-on-year terms is likely to be "somewhat overshot". Year-on-year inflation was at 15.3 percent in April, down from 18.5 percent in December 1996.
"Given wide spread backward-looking indexation, bringing it down to single digit levels by end-1998 will be all the more difficult," the OECD report said.

It said Poland's current account gap, already at $1.49 billion in March against $1.35 billion in the whole of 1996, is likely to widen further in 1997 and 1998 on rising real incomes and the cutting OF tariffs by five percent at the start of 1997.
However, the impact of the lower tariffs and higher wages would be mitigated by a "softer exchange rate policy rule" which would help exports.

"The monthly rate of depreciation (of the zloty against a basket of currencies) is assumed by the OECD secretariat to be cut to 0.9 percent (from the current one percent) in mid-1997 and to 0.8 percent at the begining of 1998," the report said. "A distinct risk, however, is that the current account gap would increase too quickly and too soon," it said.

The report said that progress with Poland's structural reforms, needed to sustain rapid growth over the medium term was uneven last year but noted the country's mass privatisation programme was on track.

"However, the restructuring of state-owned enterpries and pension reform were lagging and may be inhibited in 1997 by the polictical cycle -- parliamentary elections are due by September," the report said.
